frontmatter_description: Direct-route macro for scenes where one character models another character's understanding, including second-order belief and common knowledge.
title: Second-Order Mind and Common Knowledge
use_when: Use when the answer depends on how one character represents another character's belief, ignorance, or likely inference.
Use when shared knowledge, mutual awareness, or "who knows that who knows" is central to the scene.
Use when the scene asks where someone thinks another person will look, act, or search.
Use when nested belief is the deciding factor even if the surface story also contains a false-belief cue.
do_not_use_when: Do not use when the main task is only first-order false belief about reality with no model of another mind.
Do not use when the core issue is appearance versus reality rather than nested belief.
Do not use when the question is primarily about a nonverbal cue, emotion, pragmatics, or persuasion.

Do not use when a single narrower capability fully explains the scene (for example, just tracking one person's perceptual access, one person's emotion, or the literal meaning of an utterance) without any character modeling another character's mind.
decision_variable: how one character understands another character's understanding
direct_route_rule: Route immediately when one mind models another mind or shared knowledge is central.
trigger_checklist: One character must reason about another character's belief, expectation, or ignorance.
The answer changes if you track an embedded belief such as A thinks that B thinks X.
Shared knowledge, mutual awareness, or public vs private knowledge is relevant to the outcome.
The scene asks about expected search, expected action, or expected reaction based on another person's mistaken or shared model.
A first-order belief may be present, but it is not sufficient to answer correctly.
workflow: Identify the two minds: the OUTER mind A (whose belief the question ultimately asks for) and the INNER mind B (the person A is reasoning about). Confirm the question is nested, of the form 'what does A think B believes / where does A think B will look', not merely 'what does B believe'.

Establish B's own belief from B's perceptual access: did B see the change or move? If B was absent or could not see it, B holds a false belief fixed at the original state; if B saw it, B's belief is true and current.
Establish what A knows about B's access: does A know whether B saw the change? A's model of B is built from A's knowledge of what B could perceive, not from the real state of the world.

Answer A's belief about B's belief by combining the two: if A knows B did not see the change, A expects B to act on the OLD (false) state; if A knows B did see it, A expects B to act on the NEW (true) state. Predict the search location or expected content from this nested state, never from ground-truth reality.

For a common-knowledge or mutual-awareness question, additionally check BOTH directions: that each party knows the fact AND that each party knows the other knows it. Only when both hold is the fact mutually known, which erases any false belief; if either direction fails, one side still holds a private or false belief and you must track it.

special_case.title: Common knowledge versus private belief
special_case.rule: When both characters know the same fact and also know that the other knows it, the relevant variable is not simple belief but mutual awareness; the false belief is erased on both sides, so answer from the shared epistemic state. But if only one direction holds (one knows, yet does not know the other knows), a private or false belief survives and must still be tracked.

worked_example.scene: Mia and Theo both see the cabbage in the handbag. Theo leaves the bedroom. While Theo is away, Mia moves the cabbage to the backpack; Theo does not see this.
worked_example.question: Where does Mia think Theo will look for the cabbage first?
worked_example.answer_logic: Outer mind is Mia, inner mind is Theo. Theo's access: he was absent during the move, so Theo's belief is false and fixed at the handbag (the original place). Mia's knowledge of Theo's access: Mia knows Theo did not see the move. Combining, Mia expects Theo to search the handbag, even though the cabbage is really in the backpack. The answer follows Theo's false belief as Mia represents it, never ground-truth reality. (Contrast: if the question instead asked where Theo himself will look, the answer would also be the handbag, but that is a first-order question, not this nested one.)

boundary_exit_rule: If the question asks only where one character will look or what one character believes based on that same character's OWN first-order false belief, with no second character's mind modeled, solve it as a plain first-order false-belief problem: track only that one character's perceptual access and the original state. Do not nest. Decisive test: the question is 'where will X look', not 'where does A think X will look'.

If the twist is only that an object's appearance misleads about its real identity or contents, with no character modeling another character's mind, treat it as an appearance-versus-reality problem: separate how the thing looks from what it actually is. That is not nested belief.

If the answer depends on the intended meaning of a gesture, glance, or other nonverbal signal rather than on who-thinks-what, interpret the social cue's communicative intent; do not force a nested-belief reading.
If the answer depends on a hidden, masked, or atypical emotion rather than on one mind's model of another mind, reason about the felt-versus-displayed emotion instead of about embedded belief.
When the scene genuinely nests A-thinks-B-thinks, keep explicit bookkeeping of the two belief layers so the inner and outer beliefs are not collapsed into one.
When the scene turns on whether a fact is mutually known versus privately known, explicitly test both directions of awareness (each knows, and each knows the other knows) before answering.

When the inner character's certainty level (sure, unsure, or guessing) changes the predicted action, carry that confidence level through the nested reasoning rather than treating the inner belief as flatly true or false.
When the inner character's belief depends on how reliable the source of their information is, factor source reliability into what that inner mind is taken to believe.

references.route_signal: The scene contains embedded belief, such as who thinks what about whom, or whether a fact is mutually known, privately known, or known to be known.
hard_boundary: First-order false belief without nested belief
shortcut_to_avoid: Do not jump straight to reality; preserve each character's represented knowledge state.
Do not collapse second-order belief into the outer character's direct belief.
Do not treat common knowledge as merely duplicated private knowledge.
Do not use emotion or cue interpretation shortcuts when the question is about who thinks what.
common_failure_modes: Answering from ground-truth reality (omniscience leak) instead of from the character's model of another mind

The coincidence trap: routing on the landed answer instead of the question structure. When a character did not see the change, the second-order answer (what A thinks B believes) often numerically coincides with the first-order answer (what B believes), but the two require different reasoning; deciding a question is first-order just because the answer matches the old location is the error. Always route on whether the question embeds one mind inside another.
Flattening second-order belief into the outer character's own first-order belief, so A's model of B collapses into what A believes
Ignoring whether A knows that B was or was not informed of the change
Treating a mutually known fact as if a false belief still survives, or treating one-sided knowledge as if it were common knowledge

minimal_pair.case: Both characters see an object in its first place; one character leaves, the other moves it while the first is away, and the question asks where the mover thinks the absent character will look for it.
minimal_pair.why_it_matches: The question is nested: it asks for one character's model of another character's belief. The mover knows the absent character did not see the move, so the mover expects a search at the original place. This is the in-scope second-order case.

minimal_pair.case: The same change occurs, but the question instead asks where the absent character himself will look for the object after returning.
minimal_pair.why_it_matches: Near miss, not in scope: this is a single-level question about the absent character's OWN false belief and action, with no character modeling another character's mind. Note the trap: its correct answer (the original place) coincides with the second-order answer above, yet it is solved by the plain first-order false-belief procedure, not by nesting one mind inside another. Route on the nested question form, not on the matching answer.

boundary_stress_test: If B knows the truth but A does not know that B knows the truth, this still belongs here when the question asks what A thinks B believes or will do, because A is still modeling B's mind from A's (incorrect) view of B's access.

If the question asks only where a character will search based on that character's own mistaken belief, with no second mind being modeled, it is a first-order false-belief problem and should not be solved by nesting.
If the only twist is a misleading appearance and no character models another character's mind, it is an appearance-versus-reality problem and does not belong here.
references.generalization_note: Treat this as a reusable prototype for nested belief and mutual awareness, not as a one-off trick; any scene with explicit mind-in-mind reasoning or shared knowledge can route directly here.

validation_seed.positive_pattern: One character predicts another character's belief-based action by tracking what that other character knows, thinks, or fails to know.
validation_seed.near_miss_pattern: A character has a false belief about reality, but no one models another person's belief.
validation_seed.boundary_pattern: A fact is visible to both characters, and the question is whether that fact is mutually known, privately known, or known to be known.

notes: Keep the core variable centered on nested belief, not on a generic social bundle.

Bring in the narrower repair capabilities (recursive-belief bookkeeping, mutual-knowledge testing, inner-confidence tracking, source-reliability weighting) only for diagnosis or boundary repair, not as the primary route.
This macro should remain directly routable for scenes about who thinks what about whom.
core_question: how one character understands another character's understanding
